summary: Discusses how the Path Computation Element applies to point-to-multipoint traffic engineering in MPLS and GMPLS networks. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A one-to-many tree, where one router feeds several destinations, is much harder to plan than a single path, and planning it can overload the router that would otherwise do the job. This RFC looks at whether handing that work to a dedicated planning server makes sense, and how the work can be split up.

questions: point to multipoint mpls te path computation
what is pce applicability for p2mp
how does point to multipoint path computation work
why do routers need help computing p2mp paths
how do pce work together for large trees
subtitle: Why a network operator may hand the job of building a one-to-many tree to a dedicated planning server instead of doing it on the routers.

tldr.problem: Computing the paths for a one-to-many tree is far harder than computing a single path, and the routers at the edge of the network may not have the processing power to do it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC examines the PCE architecture for point-to-multipoint traffic engineering, covering offline and online computation, splitting the tree into fragments, and central replication points.
tldr.outcome: It defines no protocol. It concludes that P2MP computation should generally be offloaded to dedicated PCEs, and that PCE selection should take the capabilities of each PCE into account.

today: RFC 5671 is an Informational memo published in October 2009, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It examines which parts of the PCE architecture of RFC 4655 fit point-to-multipoint traffic engineering; it defines no protocol, and the protocol extensions it relies on are described elsewhere.

sections.title: Why One-to-Many Trees Are Hard to Plan
sections.content:
The Path Computation Element (PCE) defined in RFC 4655 is an entity that computes a network path or route from a network graph, applying computational constraints. The intention is that it computes the paths of traffic engineered Label Switched Paths (TE LSPs) in MPLS and GMPLS networks. RFC 4655 also defines deployment models that place PCEs differently: they may sit on the Label Switching Routers themselves, be part of the management system that asks for LSPs to be established, or stand alone as one or more computation servers in the network.

Requirements for point-to-multipoint (P2MP) MPLS TE LSPs are in RFC 4461, and the signalling extensions for setting them up are in RFC 4875. The networks are considered in this document in support of features such as layer 3 multicast VPNs and video distribution.

Choosing the paths for a P2MP tree starts with choosing the branch points. That selection is constrained by the network topology and the available resources, and it is also driven by the objective function applied to the computation. One standard objective is to minimise the total cost of the tree, the sum of the cost of every link it traverses, which produces what is known as a Steiner tree. Another common objective requires the cost of reaching each leaf of the tree to be minimised.

Two things make the job harder. Not every router in the network can perform branching functions, and that fact may be recorded in the Traffic Engineering Database (TED) the PCE uses, possibly distributed through extensions to the Interior Gateway Protocol as in RFC 5073. And network policy may dictate how branching should behave, for instance that no branch router should handle more than a given number of downstream branches for any one LSP. That might come from the replication mechanism at the routers being a round-robin copying process that delays each downstream branch by the time taken to replicate onto the previous ones, or from an administrative wish to concentrate replication on specific key nodes behaving like IP multicast rendezvous points, so that policing of receivers is easier or that protection and resiliency are simpler to implement.

Path computation for P2MP TE LSPs is therefore a significant challenge. Finding disjoint protection paths adds considerably to it, and a small change to a tree, such as adding or removing one leaf, can completely change the optimal path. Reoptimising a network holding several P2MP TE LSPs needs considerable computational resources. An ingress LSR might therefore not have the processing power for the job, and even if it did, the act of computing might get in the way of the control and management work that keeps existing LSPs running. The PCE architecture offers a way to offload those computations.
sections.plainLanguage: The hard part of a one-to-many tree is deciding where it splits. Topology, spare capacity, the shape the operator wants and which routers can copy traffic at all all have a say, and a change of one destination can move the whole tree.

sections.title: Where the Computation Should Run
sections.content:
Offline computation happens ahead of time, before LSP setup is requested, so it is requested by or performed as part of a management application. The RFC says this model suits long-lived LSPs, such as those in a transport network, and planned responses to network failures, where more planning is normally a feature of LSP provisioning. It also suits an operator who wants to keep full manual control of where LSPs sit, using the PCE purely as a calculation tool rather than as part of an automated network. Offline computation can also run in the background to reoptimize, deciding whether and when the current LSP placements have become significantly sub-optimal.

Online computation is performed on demand, when LSRs in the network decide they need to know the paths to use, so each computation is triggered by a request from an LSR. The path computation function may be collocated with the LSR making the request, or it may live in a computation-capable PCE server: another LSR in the network, a dedicated server, or a functional component of a network management system. It need not be a single PCE working alone; the result may come from cooperation between several PCEs.

Two pressures shape the choice. The first is the load on the router doing the computation. Computing a least-cost-to-leaf tree costs roughly the same as computing a single optimal path to each leaf in turn, while computing a Steiner tree costs approximately an order of magnitude more, although algorithms exist that approximate Steiner trees in roughly the same order of magnitude of time as a least-cost-to-leaf tree. Many routers cope easily with a Constrained Shortest Path First computation for a single point-to-point LSP, but they are quickly swamped if asked for many at once, as happens when recovering from a network failure. An overloaded router may no longer give timely answers for simple services, and its processing may be diverted from maintaining the control plane protocols that support existing LSPs and forwarding state. It is clearly important that existing traffic is not disrupted by the computation of a path for a new LSP. Requiring every ingress router to be powerful enough for P2MP computation is not acceptable, because in every other sense the ingress to a P2MP LSP is an ordinary ingress router. The RFC's conclusion is that P2MP computations should be offloaded to remotely located PCEs, running on dedicated or high-capacity elements such as dedicated servers or high-end routers placed as Autonomous System Border Routers.

The second pressure is overload at the PCE itself. Since P2MP computations are resource-intensive, introducing them into an established PCE network may overload the PCEs, with P2MP computations blocking other point-to-point ones. Measures exist within the architecture: LSRs can assign priorities to the requests they issue, so that P2MP requests are given lower priority and point-to-point requests are serviced first, and PCEs can apply local and network-wide policy to dictate specific processing rules. Ultimately a network must hold enough computation resources for its needs, which the architecture achieves simply by increasing the number of PCEs. Once there are enough, the LSRs may choose between them and use the overload notifications the PCEs supply to spot which are busy, and a PCE that is becoming overloaded may redistribute its queue of computation requests to less burdened PCEs.

Choice also depends on what each PCE can do. Only some PCEs in a network are likely to have the ability to perform P2MP computations at all, since that requires advanced functionality. Some of those may satisfy one objective function, such as least cost to destination, but not another, such as Steiner, and some may not support the more complex P2MP reoptimization. The architecture lets an LSR discover PCE capabilities at the same time it discovers their existence, with more detailed exchanges possible directly between PCEs and LSRs, so that a Path Computation Client can select the PCE best able to answer its requests.
sections.plainLanguage: The work can be done ahead of time by a management system, or on demand by a router asking a planning server. Because the calculation is heavy, the routers should not be doing it themselves, and the planning servers have to be able to choose between themselves when some are too busy.

sections.title: Splitting the Tree Across Several PCEs
sections.content:
A way to reduce the burden of computing a large P2MP tree on a single PCE is to fragment or partition it. This is most obvious in a multi-domain network, with several routing areas, but it applies just as well inside one domain.

The RFC's example has a P2MP LSP from ingress LSR A to egress LSRs s, t, u, v, w, x, y and z. With a single PCE model, LSR A requests the whole tree and the PCE supplies it. Alternatively, the PCE that A consults may compute only the first fragment, for example from A to K, L and M, and rely on other PCEs to compute the three smaller trees from K to t, u and v, from L to w and x, and from M to s, y and z. The LSR consulted by A may simply return that first subtree and leave LSRs K, L and M to invoke PCEs in their turn to complete the signalling. Alternatively the first PCE may cooperate with other PCEs to collect the paths for the later subtrees and return them all in a single response; the RFC notes that the mechanisms for both approaches are described in the PCE architecture.

A further possibility is that the LSRs at which the subtrees are stitched together, K, L and M here, are selected from a set of candidates using a cooperative PCE technique such as the Backward Recursive Path Computation mechanism of RFC 5441. If K, L and M were Autonomous System Border Routers or Area Border Routers, that technique would be particularly applicable.

The RFC ends this section with a caution. While these mechanisms look beneficial, it is far from obvious how the first LSR selects the transit LSRs K, L and M, or how the leaf nodes are assigned below particular downstream nodes. The computation to answer those questions may be no less intensive than determining the full tree, unless there is some known property of the leaf node identifiers, such as might come from address aggregation.
sections.plainLanguage: One big calculation can be split into smaller ones. But choosing where to split it is itself a hard calculation, and the RFC warns that splitting does not automatically make things easier.

sections.title: Central Replication Points
sections.content:
One deployment model for P2MP LSPs uses centralised, well-known replication points. The choice may be made for administrative or security reasons, or because of hardware capability limits in the network. The model can also be built without using P2MP MPLS-TE at all, by using point-to-point LSPs between the ingress and each replication point, and between each replication point and each leaf, which together deliver a P2MP service.

The RFC's example has a P2MP service from ingress LSR a to egress LSRs m, n, o and p, with four replication-capable LSRs in the network: D, E, J and K. When LSR a consults a PCE it could be given the whole P2MP path to the leaves, but in this model the PCE simply returns a point-to-point path to the first replication point, here LSR D. LSR D then consults a PCE in its turn and works out the point-to-point LSPs to egress LSRs m and p, and the point-to-point LSP to the next replication point, LSR J. Finally LSR J uses a PCE to determine the point-to-point LSPs to egresses n and o.

In this model of operation the PCE function is quite likely to sit at the replication points, which will be high-capacity LSRs. The main feature of the computation is the selection of the replication points: why LSR D rather than LSR E, and why LSR J rather than LSR K. That selection may be made purely on the basis of path optimisation, as it would be for a P2MP computation, but it may also be influenced by policy, for example because LSR D may give better protection against rogue leaf attachment, or by network loading concerns, for example because LSR E may already be handling a very large amount of traffic replication for other P2MP services.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of building a real branching tree, the service can run through a few well-known copying points. The planner's job then becomes choosing which copying points to use, which may be about security or load rather than about the shortest path.

sections.title: Reoptimization, Repair and Disjoint Paths
sections.content:
Once established, a P2MP LSP is more sensitive to modification than its point-to-point counterpart. Removing an egress from a point-to-point LSP tears the whole LSP down, but egresses are added to and removed from active P2MP LSPs as receivers come and go. Removing one needs no new path computation, because the tree can be pruned automatically. Adding one can be handled as the computation of a suitable branch point and of a point-to-point path from that branch point to the new egress, which is a relatively simple computation and can be achieved by reverse-path CSPF, much as some multicast IP routing protocols do.

Repeated addition and removal will almost certainly leave the LSP sub-optimal, because the tree shape that was right for the original destinations is distorted and is not right for the new set. The path may also become sub-optimal as resources change because other LSPs are released or new resources come online. Computing a new optimal path is as simple as computing any optimal P2MP path, but selecting one that can be applied inside the network as a migration from the existing LSP may be more complex. The administrator may apply extra constraints so that only subsets of the egresses, or subtrees of the tree, are optimised at a time, in which case the computational load may be considerable, though reoptimization can be run as a background activity. Splitting the tree into subtrees may further reduce the load and help with partial reoptimization. Network-wide reoptimization of multiple LSPs, as in RFC 5557, can achieve far greater improvements in an overloaded network than reoptimizing LSPs one at a time, and would typically be performed offline with a dedicated processor such as a PCE invoked by the network management system.

Repair is a different job. LSP repair is needed when a fault stops an LSP delivering data to an egress. For a P2MP LSP a fault is, statistically, likely to affect only a small subset of the egresses, so repair does not need to recompute the whole tree. It needs to find new branches quickly that can be grafted onto the existing tree to reconnect the disconnected leaves. Immediately after a failure there may be a very large number of computations needed to restore several LSPs, the PCEs will be heavily loaded, and it is important that computation requests are restricted to the essential. The simple repair computation can therefore achieve a first repair, while the more sophisticated reoptimization computations are deferred until the network is stable and the load on the PCEs has dropped.

Disjoint paths are required for end-to-end protection services and sometimes for load balancing. They may be fully disjoint, except at the ingress and egress, link disjoint, which allows common nodes, or best-effort disjoint, which allows shared links or nodes when no other path can be found. Computing them sequentially can lead to blocking problems where the second path cannot be placed, and these are more readily avoided if the paths are computed in parallel. Computing link-disjoint point-to-point paths is already non-trivial and the sort of task an LSR offloads to a PCE. Computing disjoint P2MP paths is considerably harder and is a good candidate for a PCE with dedicated resources, to the point that not all P2MP-capable PCEs may handle disjoint path requests, making selection between PCEs by capability necessary.

The manageability considerations are broadly those of the point-to-point case, with extra implications for the size of the requests and the extra loading they put on the PCEs. Individual PCEs may choose not to be capable of P2MP computation, an operator may disable the function, and it may be withdrawn automatically when the PCE becomes loaded. A PCE may also refuse a P2MP request or pass it on to another PCE. The requests also need considerably more information exchange than point-to-point ones, which makes the data sets larger and affects the usefulness of management data models such as MIB modules, and NETCONF with NETMOD could be considered.
sections.plainLanguage: Adding or removing one destination from a tree is easy, but the tree slowly becomes the wrong shape. Fixing it is a background job, and after a failure the priority is to reconnect the few branches that dropped rather than to rebuild everything.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states that using a PCE to compute P2MP paths raises no additional security issues beyond those that generally apply to the PCE architecture, and points to RFC 4655 for the full discussion.

It adds one warning. P2MP computation requests are more CPU-intensive and use more link bandwidth, so a PCE attacked by the injection of spurious path computation requests would be more vulnerable through a smaller number of those requests. The use of message integrity and authentication mechanisms within the PCE protocol should therefore be used to mitigate attacks from devices that are not authorised to send requests, and it would be possible to consider applying different authorisation policies for P2MP requests compared with other requests.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new is said about security here, except that a tree computation is expensive, so a flood of fake requests hurts more than it would otherwise.

viz.caption: FOUR WAYS TO SPLIT A P2MP TREE ACROSS PCES

items.title: One PCE, whole tree
items.text: LSR A asks for the entire tree and the PCE returns it in one answer.

items.title: First fragment only
items.text: The first PCE returns the subtree from A to K, L and M, and those routers ask other PCEs in turn.

items.title: Cooperating PCEs
items.text: The first PCE gathers the later subtrees from other PCEs and returns everything in a single response.

items.title: Chosen stitch points
items.text: The points where the subtrees join are picked with a cooperative technique such as backward recursive path computation.
